newsitem.title: USA: Judge rules for Time Warner in NYC dispute.
newsitem.headline: Judge rules for Time Warner in NYC dispute.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Time Warner Inc. won a major court battle Wednesday when a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction that stops New York City from airing Rupert Murdoch's Fox News on a city-run cable television channel.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that the city had violated Time Warner's First Amendment rights under the U.S. Constitution by trying to force Time Warner to carry the Fox programming and interfere with its editorial discretion.

She said New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani planned to air Fox News on a city-run cable channel in order to pressure Time Warner to carry it on a commercial station. Time Warner provides cable service to 1.1 million customers in New York.
The order also prevents New York City from airing Bloomberg Information Television on a city-run channel.
"Time Warner has a right under the First Amendment to be free from government interference with its programming decisions," Cote wrote.

"I find that the City ... has acted to compel Time Warner to add Fox News to its system of commercial channels and that these actions have had a direct, immediate and chilling effect on Time Warner's exercise of its constitutionally-protected editorial discretion."

Cote also said the city's efforts to air commercial 24-hour news programmes on so-called PEG channels designated for "public, educational and governmental" use was unprecedented and never contemplated by Congress in the Federal Cable Act.
New York City said it would appeal.
"The City of New York is going to be able to make new law about just what appropriate use of a PEG channel is," said Paul Crotty, New York City corporation counsel.

The National Cable Television Association, however, praised the decision. "We're pleased the federal court has reaffirmed Congress' decision that city governments may not impose their specific programming choices on cable operators."

The dispute centres on the role of the city's five stations, known as Crosswalks. Giuliani decided to place the new 24-hour Fox programming without commercials on one of the Crosswalks channels after Time Warner rejected it. He also planned to run Bloomberg's news programming.

Time Warner sued the city, alleging that Giuliani was acting on behalf of Murdoch's News Corp. Ltd., which owns the New York Post and WNYW-TV. It said in its suit that the city was acting as Murdoch's "latest political puppet."

"This case concerns the power of a city to influence, control and even coerce the programming decision of an operator of a cable television system. It therefore goes to the heart of First Amendment concerns" Cote wrote in her 106-page ruling.

She said that if Fox News were broadcast on Crosswalks it would build viewer loyalty. When it decides to leave because of lack of advertising revenue "it will leave Time Warner with the choice of carrying Fox News on its commercial channels or angering viewers."

Cote said the pivotal event in the case occurred on Oct. 1 when the city proposed to Time Warner that the city give up a PEG channel if Time Warner would place the new Fox News programme on one of its commercial cable channels.
Time Warner refused to "swap" channels with the city to accommodate Fox News, Cote wrote.

"Unwilling to accept Time Warner's decision, a decision protected by the First Amendment and a federal statute, the City raised the ante over the ensuing days in an effort to convince Time Warner to change its mind," Cote wrote.
She said the campaign culminated on Oct. 10 when the city placed Bloomberg Information Television on one of its PEG channels and prepared to place Fox News on another PEG channel.

The city had argued that it had not tried to interfere with Time Warner's editorial control, but had acted to expand the "diversity of voices" contributing to news, information and public affairs programming. It also said its proposal was aimed at providing more jobs in the New York area.
Cote said that the city's arguments were "entirely unconvincing."
Instead she said a "substantial and motivating" factor in the city's plan to put Fox and Bloomberg on Crosswalks, was to compel Time Warner to run Fox on a commercial channel.

"The conclusion is inescapable that the city's intonation of the rubric 'diversity' is a thinly disguised reference to its preference for the editorial content of Fox News. As such, this rationale for the City's actions cannot constitute a permissable purpose for its actions," Cote wrote.
